The problem is finding that boundary without checking every candidate. A linear scan over n elements, or over R candidate answers to a question such as the smallest battery capacity that gets a robot through its route, costs O(n) or O(R); halving the range on each step costs O(log n) or O(log R) instead, one candidate checked at a time rather than all of them.
The mechanism only needs the predicate to be true, then false, across the range, which is why it works for

The boundary conditions are where this goes wrong under pressure.

And the predicate has to actually be partitioned: running the same loop on data sorted the wrong way, or on a rotated array, returns some position with no error, because nothing checks that assumption for you.
You meet exactly this in the interview question itself, finding the first occurrence of a value by moving
down instead of stopping at the first match, and the half-open invariant is what you say out loud to show the loop, and its boundary, are correct.
